  ## Security Architecture Expert (ARM TrustZone / TPM / SMMU / IPC)

  1. **TrustZone split on QEMU (Normal + Secure worlds).**
     Use the `virt` board with TrustZone: `-machine virt,secure=on` and boot TF-A + OP-TEE artifacts 
  (BL1/BL31/BL32) to get EL3/secure world; this is the standard way to model Normal/TEE separation on 
  aarch64. ([GitLab][1], [ScienceDirect][2], [GitHub][3])

  2. **TPM 2.0 for measured boot.**
     Run a software TPM (`swtpm`) and plumb it into QEMU via `-tpmdev emulator,...` and `-device 
  tpm-crb-device,tpmdev=tpm0` (CRB is the modern MMIO interface). Extend PCRs from your bootloader and 
  persist an event log for attestation. ([Ubuntu Community Hub][4], [GitLab][5])

  3. **IOMMU/SMMU + virtio-iommu.**
     Model DMA isolation with either `-machine iommu=smmuv3` (hardware-like SMMUv3) or `-device 
  virtio-iommu-pci` (paravirtual). In-kernel, gate DMA map/unmap on capability-scoped IOVA domains. 
  ([GitLab][1], [Arm Documentation Service][6])

  4. **Capability-based kernel (EROS/seL4 style).**
     Adopt a CSpace + capability derivation/revocation discipline; treat endpoints, frames, DMA domains, 
  and AI sessions as kernel objects that are only reachable via caps. This mirrors seL4’s formally-verified
   capability model. ([seL4][7], [Wikipedia][8])

  5. **Side-channel mitigations that translate to real HW.**
     Harden hot paths against Spectre (fences on bounds-dependent accesses, constant-time crypto) and keep 
  KPTI-style split mappings for user/kernel in test images to measure cost. The Spectre literature + 
  Linux’s mitigation docs guide what’s meaningful to emulate. ([School of Computing Science][9], [Kernel 
  Docs][10])

  6. **Secure IPC with verification hooks.**
     Use capability-guarded endpoints with bounded messages and shared-frame transfer for zero-copy. The 
  seL4 IPC model is the best blueprint for minimal-surface, verifiable IPC semantics. ([seL4][7])

  7. **Crypto acceleration in QEMU.**
     Prototype offload with `virtio-crypto` while keeping kernel implementations aligned to NIST (e.g., 
  AES-GCM per SP 800-38D). ([Stack Overflow][11], [Linux Foundation Wiki][12])

  8. **Attack-surface minimization.**
     Apply SDL practices: aggressively trim drivers and syscalls for the QEMU profile, threat-model each 
  exposed interface, and enforce secure defaults. ([ejaaskel - Embedded Software Handyman][13])

  9. **Runtime security monitoring.**
     Leverage QMP + in-guest hooks to stream kernel events into a security monitor; isomorphic to DARPA 
  CGC-style continuous assessment, but aimed at your cap checks and policy violations. ([Ten Forums][14])

  10. **Formal-methods on Rust.**
      Target proofs around cap invariants and selected `unsafe` blocks using Prusti (deductive) and Kani 
  (bit-precise model checking via CBMC). Start with small specs (no panics, ownership invariants) and 
  expand. ([ETH Zurich PM][15], [GitHub][16])

  ---

  ## Machine Learning Systems Architect (TinyML / NPU stubs / RT inference)

  1. **TinyML in kernel space.**
     Embed a static-arena TFLite-Micro-class runtime (int8, fixed-point ops), keep the fast path 
  alloc-free, and store model blobs in a versioned, hashed ELF section. TFLM docs cover footprint & 
  constraints. ([Medium][17], [Arm Documentation Service][6])

  2. **NPU emulation strategy.**
     There’s no out-of-the-box Ethos-N emulation; build an MMIO “fake NPU” (registers, doorbells, IRQ) or a
   TCG plugin that triggers interrupts and copies buffers—good enough to validate driver/ABI. 
  ([qemu.readthedocs.io][18])

  3. **<10 µs inference budget (emulated).**
     Use deterministic execution (`icount`/record-replay) for repeatable latency tests; reserve CPU and 
  avoid page faults. For policy, borrow PREEMPT\_RT ideas (priority scheduling & IRQ threading) even if 
  you’re not on Linux. ([qemu.org][19], [lwn.net][20])

  4. **Federated learning across QEMU nodes.**
     Implement FedAvg rounds (client sampling, local SGD, aggregation) and add secure aggregation later; 
  this maps well to a TAP/bridge network of VMs. ([Proceedings of Machine Learning Research][21], 
  [arXiv][22])

  5. **Edge-style data paths.**
     For ultra-low overhead in/out of the kernel ML path, use zero-copy iovecs and cache-friendly message 
  layouts; Demikernel’s us-scale datapath lessons are directly applicable. ([irenezhang.net][23])

  6. **Neuromorphic concepts (event-driven).**
     Prototype event-driven kernels (interrupt-oriented activation, sparse compute) inspired by Intel Loihi
   results to test kernel schedulers for spiking-style bursts. ([think.in2p3.fr][24], 
  [dynamicfieldtheory.org][25])

  7. **Compression for kernel-space models.**
     Apply pruning + quantization (int8) and pack activations to align with your DMA/iovec boundaries to 
  keep the RT path branch-predictable; TinyML surveys capture the trade-offs. ([arXiv][26])

  8. **Adaptive/online learning.**
     Gate any in-kernel updates behind capability-scoped “training sessions”, then re-verify checksums and 
  roll back on drift to keep the trusted boot chain intact (design aligns with FL/secure-agg literature). 
  ([arXiv][22])

  9. **Privacy-preserving ML.**
     Layer DP mechanisms (per-round noise) on FL rounds; start with language-model DP recipes and move to 
  image workloads. ([arXiv][27])

  10. **HW/SW co-design path.**
      The QEMU-fake-NPU ABI you validate here becomes the contract for future real accelerators; keep the 
  queue format, doorbells, and error codes stable.

  ---

  ## Operating Systems Research Expert (SMP / NUMA / Scheduling / Microkernel)

  1. **SMP bring-up on aarch64.**
     Boot APs via PSCI `CPU_ON`, use per-CPU stacks, and drive IPIs via GICv3; on QEMU: `-smp N -machine 
  gic-version=3`. ([Kernel.org][28])

  2. **NUMA in QEMU.**
     Model memory locality with `-numa node,memdev=...` and per-node memory-backends to exercise 
  first-touch and page migration policies. ([GitLab][1])

  3. **Lock-free building blocks.**
     Adopt MPMC rings and sequence counters for read-mostly telemetry—your baseline per Herlihy & Shavit’s 
  guidelines.

  4. **Scheduling experiments.**
     Run a hybrid: CFS-like for best-effort + fixed-priority RT queues for inference; expose a BPF-like 
  policy hook for research scheduling in userland test builds (inspiration: CFS/BPF).

  5. **Microkernel boundary.**
     You’re already cap-based; keep drivers and file/cache services out of the TCB. seL4 is the reference 
  point for a high-assurance microkernel you can emulate. ([seL4][7])

  6. **GICv3 correctness.**
     Initialize redistributors per-CPU and test SGI paths; validate against the GICv3/v4 spec while running
   on QEMU’s GICv3. ([Kib][29])

  ---

  ## Real-Time Systems Expert (Determinism / Interrupts / WCET)

  1. **Deterministic emulation for RT tests.**
     Use instruction-counting/record-replay to make latency measurements comparable across runs; pair with 
  a fixed tick source. ([qemu.org][19])

  2. **RT scheduling policy.**
     Adopt fixed-priority (RMS/DM) or EDF where appropriate; PREEMPT\_RT’s techniques (IRQ threading, 
  priority inheritance) are the pragmatic reference even if you’re not on Linux. ([Iris][30], 
  [lwn.net][20])

  3. **GICv3 latency hygiene.**
     Pin IRQs to CPUs that run the RT tasks, use SGIs for inter-task wakeups, and keep handler/DSR strictly
   bounded per the GIC spec guidance. ([Kib][29])

  4. **Deterministic memory.**
     Pre-reserve slabs for RT classes, avoid page faults, and enforce no-alloc on the hot path 
  (Xenomai/RTAI heritage).

  5. **WCET harness.**
     Instrument each kernel “AI op” with cycle windows; hard-fail on overruns and capture traces for 
  regression.

  ---

  ## Distributed Systems Architect (Consensus / Cluster / Observability)

  1. **QEMU cluster topology.**
     Bridge TAP interfaces (`br0`) and launch multiple VMs with virtio-net multiqueue (`mq=on`, 
  `vectors=2*q+2`) for throughput under SMP. ([linux-kvm.org][31])

  2. **Consensus in-kernel.**
     Prototype Raft (timers + RPC over a reliable mailbox atop virtio-net) for leader election, log 
  replication, and snapshots; ideal for deterministic replay in emulation. ([seL4][7])

  3. **Distributed storage.**
     For a PoC, pair a replicated write-ahead log with a chunk store; use leases for cache coherence 
  (inspiration: GFS/Spanner). ([SpringerLink][32], [seL4][33])

  4. **Actor-style services.**
     Model node-local services after Orleans’ virtual actors to keep fault-tolerance simple under VM 
  restarts. ([seL4][34])

  5. **Observability & tracing.**
     Emit spans/metrics from kernel tasks and collect with an OpenTelemetry agent running in a companion 
  VM. ([ResearchGate][35])

  6. **Load balancing.**
     Use Maglev-style consistent hashing in an in-kernel L4 balancer to keep flow stickiness across VM 
  restarts. ([SpringerLink][32])

  ---

  ## Performance Engineering Expert (HPC-ish tuning under QEMU)

  1. **Make the emulator go fast (within reason).**
     Enable multi-threaded TCG (`-accel tcg,thread=multi`) so each vCPU runs on its own host thread; break 
  I/O out into IOThreads for lower jitter. ([about.gitlab.com][36], [qemu.org][37])

  2. **VirtIO tuning.**
     Use multiqueue virtio-net and vhost-user where possible; set `vectors=2*q+2` and pin queues to CPUs. 
  ([linux-kvm.org][31])

  3. **Repeatable perf & regression testing.**
     Freeze QEMU version, run with deterministic clocks, and compare KPIs across builds 
  (instruction-count/record-replay is your friend). ([qemu.org][19])

  ---

  ## Rust-specific safety & implementation patterns (cross-cutting)

  * **Minimize `unsafe`, localize proofs.** Use Rust unsafe-code guidelines + Nomicon patterns, and verify 
  small `unsafe` blocks with Prusti/Kani. ([Microsoft][38], [OpenTelemetry][39], [ETH Zurich PM][15], 
  [GitHub][16])
  * **Type-state for device sessions & AI ops.** Encode state transitions in types (Created→Loaded→Running)
   to prevent misuse at compile time.
  * **Zero-copy, bounded messages.** Fixed-size, cache-aligned descriptors + shared-frame caps to keep RT 
  paths branch-predictable.
  * **Error taxonomy for AI.** Distinguish `Timeout`, `ModelHashMismatch`, `ResourceExhausted`, 
  `DeviceLost` to drive rollback/fail-closed behaviors.

  Claude opus 4.1 :
  I'll provide comprehensive guidance as each AI specialist for your SIS kernel expansion project. This is

  ## Security Architecture Expert Response

  ### 1. TrustZone Implementation in QEMU

  For TrustZone in QEMU ARM64, you'll need:

  **QEMU Configuration:**
  ```bash
  qemu-system-aarch64 \
    -machine virt,secure=on,virtualization=on \
    -cpu cortex-a57 \
    -smp 4 \
    -m 4G \
    -bios bl1.bin \
    -d guest_errors,unimp
  ```

  **Kernel Modifications:**
  - Implement separate secure/non-secure world entry points
  - Add SMC (Secure Monitor Call) handling in your exception vectors
  - Create secure monitor at EL3 with world switch capability
  - Implement TZASC (TrustZone Address Space Controller) emulation support

  ### 2. TPM 2.0 Emulation

  Use QEMU's built-in TPM support:
  ```bash
  -chardev socket,id=chrtpm,path=/tmp/swtpm-sock \
  -tpmdev emulator,id=tpm0,chardev=chrtpm \
  -device tpm-tis-device,tpmdev=tpm0
  ```

  Implement kernel-side:
  - TPM driver for measured boot
  - PCR (Platform Configuration Register) extension during boot stages
  - Attestation service interface

  ### 3. Memory Protection with SMMU

  Configure Stage-2 translation for isolation:
  ```c
  // SMMU configuration structure
  struct smmu_config {
      uint64_t ttbr0;      // Translation table base
      uint32_t tcr;        // Translation control
      uint32_t mair;       // Memory attributes
  };

  // Enable SMMU for device isolation
  void enable_smmu_protection(void) {
      // Configure stream mapping registers
      write_smmu_reg(SMMU_CR0, CR0_SMMUEN);
      // Set up context banks for different security domains
  }
  ```

  ## Machine Learning Systems Architect Response

  ### 1. TinyML Kernel Integration

  Implement a minimal inference engine:
  ```c
  // Kernel-space ML inference structure
  struct kernel_ml_model {
      uint8_t *weights;        // Quantized INT8 weights
      uint32_t *layer_config;  // Layer configurations
      void (*inference_fn)(void*);
  };

  // Real-time inference with preemption disabled
  ```

  ### 3. Lock-Free Data Structures

  Implement essential lock-free primitives:
  ```c
  // Lock-free queue using CAS
  struct lockfree_queue {
      atomic_t head;
      atomic_t tail;
      void *buffer[QUEUE_SIZE];
  };

  bool lockfree_enqueue(struct lockfree_queue *q, void *item) {
      int tail, next;
      do {
          tail = atomic_read(&q->tail);
          next = (tail + 1) % QUEUE_SIZE;
          if (next == atomic_read(&q->head))
              return false; // Queue full
      } while (!atomic_cmpxchg(&q->tail, tail, next));
      
      q->buffer[tail] = item;
      return true;
  }
  ```

  ### 3. Deterministic Memory Allocation

  Implement TLSF (Two-Level Segregated Fit) allocator:
  ```c
  struct tlsf_pool {
      uint32_t fl_bitmap;
      uint32_t sl_bitmap[FL_INDEX_COUNT];
      block_header_t *blocks[FL_INDEX_COUNT][SL_INDEX_COUNT];
  };

  // O(1) allocation
  void *tlsf_malloc(struct tlsf_pool *pool, size_t size) {
      int fl, sl;
      block_header_t *block;
      
      mapping_search(size, &fl, &sl);
      block = remove_free_block(pool, fl, sl);
      
      if (block) {
          split_block(block, size);
          return block_to_ptr(block);
      }
      return NULL;
  }
  ```

  ```c
  };

  // Read PMU counters
  static inline uint64_t read_pmccntr(void) {
      uint64_t val;
      asm volatile("mrs %0, pmccntr_el0" : "=r" (val));
      return val;
  }

  // Kernel performance profiling
  void profile_function(void (*func)(void)) {
      uint64_t start = read_pmccntr();
      func();
      uint64_t end = read_pmccntr();
      
      record_performance(end - start);
  }
  ```
